title: Logging & SIEM Concept Map
subtitle: From a single log line to a confirmed incident. Tap a bubble.
searchPlaceholder: Search: e.g. CEF, sourcetype, risk score…
rootDesc: Everything a SOC knows, it knows from logs. This map follows the chain: an application writes a log, a format carries it, a SIEM collects and correlates it, a rule turns it into an alert, and an analyst decides whether it is an incident. Splunk appears here as the specific tool, but the concepts transfer to any SIEM.

modules.title: Application Logs
modules.desc: Records an application writes about its own behavior. Unlike OS or device logs, the application's own code decides what gets written — so what is missing is a development decision, not a collection failure.

children.title: Access log
children.desc: Who reached what. A web server line carries client IP, timestamp, method and URI, status code, bytes, referer, user-agent, and response time.

children.title: Error log
children.desc: Exceptions and stack traces. Useful for detection, dangerous if exposed to users — that exposure is OWASP A02.

children.title: Debug / trace log
children.desc: Verbose developer output. Left enabled in production it leaks internal paths, versions, and sometimes credentials.

children.title: What to hunt in them
children.desc: Sequential object IDs in one session (IDOR), clusters of 401/403 (brute force), spikes of 500s (injection attempts), scanner user-agents, unusual response-time patterns (time-based SQLi).

modules.title: Audit Logs
modules.desc: Who did what, when, and to what. Where an access log answers 'what happened', an audit log answers 'who is accountable' — which gives it legal and regulatory weight an ordinary log does not carry.

children.title: What belongs in one
children.desc: Account creation and deletion, permission changes, configuration changes, access to sensitive records, authentication outcomes, and business-critical transactions.

children.title: Immutability
children.desc: Append-only and stored off the originating host. An attacker who can edit the audit trail can erase the entire investigation.

children.title: Time synchronization
children.desc: NTP across every source. If clocks drift, correlation between systems silently breaks and timelines become unusable.

children.title: Retention
children.desc: Banking regulation drives retention measured in years, not days — and drives which index the data lands in.

children.title: Examples
children.desc: AWS CloudTrail, Windows Security Event Log, Linux auditd, database audit trails.

modules.title: Syslog
modules.desc: Both a transport protocol and a format — the long-standing default for network devices and Unix systems. Sent over UDP 514, TCP 514, or TLS 6514.

children.title: Structure
children.desc: Priority (facility plus severity), version, timestamp, hostname, app name, PID, message ID, structured data, then the message.

children.title: The free-text problem
children.desc: The message body is not standardized. Extracting a username from a sentence requires a regex, and every vendor phrases it differently — so every source needs its own parser.

children.title: Where you meet it
children.desc: Firewalls, switches, Linux hosts, appliances — anything that predates or ignores structured logging.

modules.title: CEF
modules.desc: Originally from ArcSight. Normalizes log content into standard field names, usually carried over syslog. The point is that src always means source IP, whichever vendor wrote the line.

children.title: Header
children.desc: Seven pipe-delimited fields: CEF version, device vendor, device product, device version, signature ID, name, severity.

children.title: Extension
children.desc: Key=value pairs using a standard dictionary — src, dst, spt, dpt, duser, act — which removes most of the parser-writing burden.

children.title: Flat by design
children.desc: No nesting. Simple and predictable, but it cannot express structured objects the way JSON can.

children.title: Where you meet it
children.desc: Security appliances above all — firewalls, IPS, DLP, mail gateways.

modules.title: JSON
modules.desc: Key-value structure that can nest. The default for modern applications, cloud services, and containers.

children.title: Nesting
children.desc: Related fields group naturally — a source object holding both ip and port, a geo object holding country and city.

children.title: Trade-off
children.desc: Trivially parseable and expressive, but the largest on the wire since every key repeats on every event, which costs ingestion volume.

children.title: Field naming
children.desc: Structure is guaranteed; vocabulary is not. Schemas like ECS and OCSF exist precisely to impose a common dictionary on top.

modules.title: Format Comparison
modules.desc: The distinction in one line: syslog solves transport and leaves content free; CEF standardizes field names but stays flat; JSON is flexible and nestable but guarantees no common vocabulary.

children.title: Parseability
children.desc: Syslog needs regex; CEF and JSON parse natively. This is the single biggest practical difference when onboarding a new source.

children.title: Size on the wire
children.desc: Syslog smallest, CEF middle, JSON largest — which matters directly, because most SIEMs bill by ingested volume.

children.title: Nesting support
children.desc: Only JSON. CEF and syslog are flat, so structured data has to be flattened into extra fields.

children.title: Normalization
children.desc: Whatever arrives, the SIEM maps it into one common schema so that source IP is a single searchable field across every product.

modules.title: Recognizing Formats
modules.desc: Splunk has no log format of its own: it stores each event exactly as it arrived, in the _raw field, so every sourcetype can look different. Switch the Events view from List to Raw and match the first characters of a line against the samples below. Addresses use documentation ranges.

children.title: Syslog
children.desc: <134>Oct  5 10:12:01 web01 sshd[2211]: Accepted password for alice from 192.0.2.10 port 51514 ssh2 — a priority value in angle brackets (facility × 8 + severity), then timestamp, hostname, program and PID. Everything after the colon is free text.

children.title: CEF over syslog
children.desc: <134>Oct  5 10:12:01 fw01 CEF:0|ExampleVendor|ExampleFW|1.0|100|Connection blocked|5|src=192.0.2.10 dst=198.51.100.20 dpt=445 act=blocked — the syslog header carries it; from CEF:0 onwards is the content. Syslog is the transport and CEF the format, which is the most common way the two meet.

children.title: JSON
children.desc: {"time":"2026-10-05T10:12:01Z","user":"alice","source":{"ip":"192.0.2.10"},"action":"login","result":"success"} — braces and quoted keys, with nesting. Typical of cloud services and modern applications; Splunk extracts the fields automatically, or with | spath.

children.title: Key=value
children.desc: date=2026-10-05 time=10:12:01 type=traffic srcip=192.0.2.10 dstip=198.51.100.20 dstport=443 action=accept — flat pairs with no CEF header, each vendor choosing its own key names. Common on firewalls; Fortigate writes this way.

children.title: CSV
children.desc: 1,2026/10/05 10:12:01,001122334455,TRAFFIC,end,2561,2026/10/05 10:12:01,192.0.2.10,198.51.100.20,... — comma-separated values in a fixed order with no names. A field only means something by its position, so the vendor's add-on is needed to label it. Palo Alto's classic format.

children.title: Windows Event Log
children.desc: LogName=Security EventCode=4624 ComputerName=PC01.example.com Message=An account was successfully logged on. — multi-line text, or XML starting with <Event xmlns=...> when collected as XmlWinEventLog. The EventCode is the key field: 4624 logon, 4625 failed logon, 4688 process creation.

modules.title: SIEM
modules.desc: Security Information and Event Management — the merger of SIM (collection, storage, reporting) and SEM (real-time monitoring and alerting). It exists because EDR sees one endpoint and NDR sees the network, while an attack crosses both.

children.title: Collection
children.desc: Pulls logs from firewalls, endpoints, AD, applications, and cloud into one place.

children.title: Normalization
children.desc: Maps every format onto a shared schema, so one query works across sources that disagree about field names.

children.title: Correlation
children.desc: The real value. Individually meaningless events combine into meaning: a connection, then fifty failed logins, then one success, then that account touching a server it has never used.

children.title: Alerting
children.desc: Rules fire when a pattern matches. Logging without alerting is the specific failure OWASP renamed A09 to highlight in 2025.

children.title: Retention & compliance
children.desc: Searchable history for investigation, and the evidence trail regulators require.

children.title: The noise problem
children.desc: Tines research found the average SOC analyst received 4,484 alerts a day in 2025, and 67% went uninvestigated. Tuning is not optional.

modules.title: Event → Incident
modules.desc: Four terms that are often used loosely but describe a funnel: volume falls at each stage while meaning rises. Most of a junior analyst's day is spent at the third step deciding whether to move to the fourth.

children.title: Event
children.desc: Anything that happens on a system. It need not even be recorded — and an event that is never logged effectively did not happen, as far as the SOC is concerned.

children.title: Log
children.desc: An event that was written down and stored. Which events become logs is a configuration decision made long before the incident.

children.title: Alert
children.desc: One or more logs that matched a rule or threshold and were raised for attention.

children.title: Incident
children.desc: An alert that investigation confirmed to be a real security event. Not every alert becomes one — closing false positives correctly is as much the job as escalating true ones.

children.title: Triage
children.desc: The decision step between alert and incident: gather context, judge true or false positive, escalate or close with a reason.

children.title: After escalation
children.desc: Incident response begins — containment (such as isolating the host via EDR), eradication, recovery, and lessons learned.

modules.title: Splunk
modules.desc: A general-purpose machine-data platform, not only a security tool. The security product on top is Splunk Enterprise Security. Its query language, SPL, chains commands with pipes.

children.title: Forwarder
children.desc: The lightweight agent on each host that ships logs onward to an indexer.

children.title: Indexer
children.desc: Parses incoming data, assigns timestamps and metadata, indexes and stores it.

children.title: Search Head
children.desc: Where SPL queries run and dashboards live — the console an analyst actually works in.

children.title: SPL
children.desc: Pipe-chained query language: select an index, filter, aggregate with stats, filter again with where, then sort. Conceptually close to a PowerShell pipeline.

children.title: Enterprise Security
children.desc: Adds prebuilt correlation searches, notable events, the incident review screen, risk-based alerting, and MITRE ATT&CK mapping.

children.title: BOTS datasets
children.desc: Boss of the SOC — Splunk's free, public attack-scenario datasets. The practical way to learn SPL on realistic data.

modules.title: index · source · sourcetype
modules.desc: The metadata Splunk attaches to every event so it knows where data came from and how to read it. Getting these three straight is what separates a fast query from a slow one.

children.title: index
children.desc: Where the data is physically stored — a partition in the data store. Drives search performance, access control, and retention period. Start almost every search with it.

children.title: source
children.desc: The specific origin: a full file path or input point, such as a web server's access.log or a syslog port.

children.title: sourcetype
children.desc: The data's format, and the most important of the three — it tells Splunk how to parse the event: where the timestamp sits, how fields are extracted, where a line ends.

children.title: host
children.desc: Which machine the event came from. The fourth default metadata field alongside the other three.

children.title: Worked example
children.desc: Two nginx servers share one index and one sourcetype but differ by host. Add the same server's error log and index stays the same while source and sourcetype both change, because the format differs.

children.title: Query hygiene
children.desc: Always narrow by index and sourcetype first. Searching with index=* is slow and frowned on for the license and resource cost it incurs.

modules.title: Other SIEM Products
modules.desc: The vendors you will hear named alongside Splunk. Worth knowing the shape of the market, including how much of it changed hands recently.

children.title: Microsoft Sentinel
children.desc: Cloud-native on Azure, strongest fit where the estate is already Microsoft and Defender-heavy.

children.title: IBM QRadar
children.desc: Long established in regulated and banking environments; IBM sold its SaaS assets to Palo Alto Networks in 2024.

children.title: Elastic Security
children.desc: Built on the ELK stack, open-source foundation and lower cost per GB.

children.title: Falcon Next-Gen SIEM
children.desc: CrowdStrike's LogScale-based SIEM — module M8 on the Falcon map, ingesting third-party sources alongside Falcon's own telemetry.

children.title: Google SecOps (Chronicle)
children.desc: Built for very high ingestion volume with long hot retention.

children.title: Open-source options
children.desc: Wazuh and Graylog — the practical route to building a home lab and feeding it Sysmon data.

modules.title: Hands-on SPL
modules.desc: The practical half of the exercise: find out what data you can see, learn what produces it, then filter it. Field names below are typical of web proxy logs; the exact names depend on the vendor and the sourcetype, so check the field sidebar first.

children.title: Which indexes can I see?
children.desc: | eventcount summarize=false index=* lists every index your role can search. | tstats count where index=* by index gives the same with event volume, and is fast because it reads only metadata.

children.title: What is inside them?
children.desc: | tstats count where index=<name> by sourcetype, host shows which systems and log types feed an index. Each sourcetype is a clue to look up: a proxy, a firewall, a mail gateway, an identity provider.

children.title: Filter by category
children.desc: index=<proxy> category="Gambling" | stats count by user, url. Field-value pairs before the first pipe filter at search time; stats then turns raw events into a table.

children.title: Category + risk score
children.desc: index=<proxy> category="Uncategorized" risk_score>=70 | table _time user src_ip url action. Combining two conditions is what turns a noisy list into a short one worth reading — uncategorized and high-risk together is far rarer than either alone.

children.title: My own traffic
children.desc: index=<proxy> user="<your username>" earliest=-24h | stats count by domain | sort -count. You know what you actually browsed, so you can check whether the logs tell the truth.

children.title: Why do this
children.desc: Filtering your own activity is a calibration exercise: known ground truth shows what the log records, what it misses, and how a real user looks. That baseline is what makes an anomaly in someone else's traffic recognizable during an investigation.

modules.title: Investigating an IP
modules.desc: What an unknown IP looks like from inside Splunk, and the traps that make a first guess wrong. The method: search broadly, read which role the IP plays in each event, form a hypothesis, then try to disprove it before writing it down.

children.title: host vs src vs dest
children.desc: host is the machine that sent the log, often written as a hostname. src started the connection; dest received it. Searching only host=<ip> misses every log where the IP is the other end of a connection.

children.title: Search the IP as a term
children.desc: index=* TERM(<ip>) | stats count by index, sourcetype, host finds the IP in any field. Then index=* dest=<ip> | stats count by dest_port shows which services it offers, and src=<ip> what it talks to.

children.title: Read the raw event
children.desc: stats and tstats return tables, not events — run a plain search to get the Events tab. Expand an event with the arrow, click a value to add it to the search, and use Show Source to see neighbouring lines.

children.title: Visibility limits
children.desc: Splunk sees only what is collected — network traffic is often logged only where it crosses a firewall. Traffic inside one segment may never appear, so a low count can mean low visibility rather than low activity.

children.title: Not in inventory ≠ suspicious
children.desc: Server inventories usually exclude workstations, which take DHCP addresses and are tracked in EDR or AD instead. A client talking LDAP to a domain controller on 389 is normal background traffic, not a sign of a directory server.

children.title: Names and hypotheses
children.desc: Abbreviations in hostnames mislead — DC can mean domain controller or data center. Treat a name as a clue, confirm with DNS (SRV records, reverse lookup), and record when a hypothesis changed and why.
